'''James Richard Arnold''' (May 5, 1923&nbsp;&ndash; January 6, 2012) was the [[Harold C. Urey]] Professor of Chemistry (emeritus), and a noted pioneer in the field of planetary and space [[chemistry]] at the [[University of California, San Diego]] (UCSD), where an endowed lectureship has been established in his name.

== Early life and education ==
Arnold received his education at [[Princeton University]], where he enrolled as an undergraduate at age 16. He earned his doctorate there in 1946 at 23, for work on the [[Manhattan Project]] (his thesis is still classified).<ref name="pnas"/> Concerns about nuclear fallout and war prompted him to be an early member of the [[Union of Concerned Scientists]]<ref name="aas">[https://aas.org/obituaries/james-r-arnold-1923-2012, James R. Arnold (1923 - 2012)] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180205125958/https://aas.org/obituaries/james-r-arnold-1923-2012|date=2018-11-19}}, Athena Coustenis for the American Astronomical Society</ref> and a [[World Federalism|World Federalist]], through which he met his wife Louise in 1950.<ref name="pnas"/>

As a [[postdoctoral researcher]] under [[Willard Libby]] at the [[University of Chicago]], Arnold helped develop the techniques for [[Radiocarbon Dating|Carbon-14 dating]], working with archeological samples from Egypt and other samples with known ages. For this work, Libby was awarded the [[Nobel Prize in Chemistry]] in 1960.<ref>[https://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/chemistry/laureates/1960/libby-lecture.pdf Radiocarbon Dating], Willard F. Libby, Nobel Lecture</ref>

== Career ==
After his postdoc, Arnold returned to Princeton as a faculty member, working on using [[cosmic rays]] to measure the age of rocks.,<ref name="aas"/> and where he began his work on extraterrestrial material, including cosmic rays. It was at Princeton that Masatake (Masa) Honda and [[Devendra Lal]] first joined his work, an association amongst them that would last the rest of their lives.<ref name="pnas"/>

In 1957, [[Roger Revelle]] was working to start [[UCSD]] near the campus of [[Scripps Institution of Oceanography]]. He recruited Arnold and a few others to be the founding faculty. The recruitment of [[Harold C. Urey]] convinced Arnold to accept and move west in 1958, leaving Princeton to become the founding chair of the UCSD Department of Chemistry and help found the campus and recruit faculty.<ref name="pnas"/><ref>[https://www.latimes.com/la-me-james-arnold-20120122-story.html "James Arnold dies at 88; pushed to unlock secrets in moon rocks"], Elaine Woo, obituary in ''The Los Angeles Times'', Jan 22, 2012.</ref><ref name="calspace">[http://calspace.ucsd.edu/casgc/JArnoldLecture/JRA_Biography.htm CalSpace Biography]</ref> He was a [[NASA]] consultant for many years, helping set scientific research priorities,<ref name="aas"/> starting just three months after NASA was founded.<ref name="ucsd">[http://physicalsciences.ucsd.edu/news/2012/jimarnold.html "Jim Arnold, founding chemistry chair, 1923-2012"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150330073125/http://physicalsciences.ucsd.edu/news/2012/jimarnold.html |date=2015-03-30 }}, Obituary, UCSD Division of Physical Sciences</ref> He played a major role in establishing and reforming the [[Lunar Receiving Laboratory]] for handling lunar samples returned during the [[Apollo program]],<ref>[http://ucsdnews.ucsd.edu/pressrelease/jim_arnold_founding_chemist_at_uc_san_diego_dies_at_88/], UC San Diego, Obituary</ref><ref>[http://curator.jsc.nasa.gov/lunar/lnews/lnjul94/hist25.htm 25 Years of Curating Moon Rocks], Judy Allton</ref> including being one of the "[[Four Horsemen (NASA)|Four Horsemen]]", along with [[Robert M. Walker (physicist)|Bob Walker]], [[Paul Werner Gast]], and [[Gerald J. Wasserburg|Gerry Wasserburg]].<ref name="ucsd"/><ref>{{cite journal |title=25 Years Of Curating Moon Rocks |journal=Lunar News |date=July 1994 |issue=57 |pages=8 |url=https://curator.jsc.nasa.gov/lunar/lnews/LNJul94/LN_57_Jul_94.pdf}}</ref>

Arnold performed his own research on lunar rocks and cosmic rays.<ref name="aas"/> Under the name SHRELLDALFF (from the initials of its members), his team produced important early papers, and he continued long afterwards with lunar studies, including measurements of the bombardment of the lunar surface by cosmic rays, helping to plot the energy output of the Sun over millions of years.<ref name="pnas"/> For his work he was awarded the [[NASA Exceptional Scientific Achievement Medal]] in 1970.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.history.nasa.gov/SP-4012/vol4/appa.htm |title=SP-4012 NASA Historical Data Book: Volume IV, "NASA Resources 1969-1978," Appendix A |access-date=2015-05-27 |archive-date=2017-12-25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171225233039/https://history.nasa.gov/SP-4012/vol4/appa.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref>

At the request of then-Governor [[Jerry Brown]], he founded the University of California's California Space Institute (CalSpace) in 1979, and was its first director for ten years,<ref name="pnas"/><ref>Obituary: "Jim Arnold, First Director of CA Space Institute, Dies at 88", ''Scientific Computing'' [http://www.scientificcomputing.com/news-DS-Jim-Arnold-First-Director-of-CA-Space-Institute-Dies-at-88-011612.aspx]</ref>

Asteroid 2143,  "[[Jimarnold]]", was named for Arnold by its discoverers, [[Eleanor Helin|E. F. Helin]] and [[Eugene Shoemaker|Gene Shoemaker]], in 1980 for his work on computer models of meteorite travel.<ref name="aas"/>

Arnold was  a member of the U.S. [[National Academy of Sciences]], the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]], and a Foreign Fellow of the [[Indian National Science Academy]].

Arnold was also known for wild shirts, a relief from the formal dress required at Princeton.<ref name="pnas">[http://www.pnas.org/content/109/12/4339.full "James R. Arnold: From the Manhattan Project to the moon and beyond"] Obituary, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences</ref>
He was married to Louise Arnold for 60 years, and they had three sons, Bob, Ted, and [[Ken Arnold|Ken]].<ref>{{cite web|last=Brown|first=Susan|title=Jim Arnold, Founding Chemist at UC San Diego Dies at 88|url=http://ucsdnews.ucsd.edu/pressreleases/jim_arnold_founding_chemist_at_uc_san_diego_dies_at_88/}}</ref>
